title: Can you sweat colors?
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss sweating, starting with the two types of sweat glands (eccrine and apocrine) and their functions: eccrine glands cool the body under control of the hypothalamus, while apocrine glands are linked to emotion and produce the sweat that smells once bacteria act on it. They then cover chromhidrosis, a rare condition in which sweat is colored (blue, green, yellow, black, brown for apocrine, from lipofuscin; red or other colors for eccrine, often from something ingested such as foods with pigment). They cite a nurse who sweated red for about five months, apparently from tomato paste and paprika in a prepared food, and describe how a Wood's lamp helps diagnose apocrine cases. Treatments discussed include capsaicin cream (which may reduce substance P activity), Botox, gland removal, and expressing glands. Later, a listener named Rachel writes in to question the hosts' lumping of Pilgrims and Puritans in the America's Murderer episode; the hosts say they are unsure and plan to look into it.

segments.title: Opening banter and birthday trip
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck chat about Chuck's upcoming birthday trip to New York and their hot summer weather, leading into the sweating topic.

segments.title: Eccrine and apocrine sweat glands
segments.summary: The hosts explain the two types of sweat glands. Eccrine glands cool the body, controlled by the hypothalamus. Apocrine glands in the armpits and breasts produce sweat that smells once skin bacteria break down its fats and wastes.

segments.title: Chromhidrosis: colored sweat
segments.summary: Chromhidrosis is introduced as a rare, benign, embarrassing condition in which sweat is colored. Apocrine cases produce yellow, green, blue, black, or brown sweat from oxidized lipofuscin, which glows under a Wood's lamp. Eccrine cases come from pigments ingested in food or other substances.

segments.title: The nurse who sweated red
segments.summary: A nurse, reportedly around 26, sweated red for about five months before seeking treatment. Doctors linked it to a tomato-and-paprika prepared food she snacked on constantly. Hosts note the science is not well understood and little research funding exists.

segments.title: Treatments for colored and excessive sweat
segments.summary: Treatment for eccrine cases is identifying and stopping the culprit food. For apocrine cases, capsaicin cream (from red pepper) may reduce substance P, which is involved in apocrine sweating. Botox, gland removal, and gland expression are also mentioned. Hosts also discuss sweating from nerves and a possible aura before it.

segments.title: Mirror dystonia and alien hand syndrome
segments.summary: Chuck mentions a blog post he wrote about mirror dystonia, which he describes as combining mirror neurons and alien hand syndrome. Both sides of the body act together due to a protein that fails to switch signals to one side.

segments.title: Dog anal glands tangent
segments.summary: The hosts briefly discuss expressing dogs' anal glands and the smell involved.

segments.title: Chuck's article and acne
segments.summary: Chuck mentions he wrote articles on sweat, zits, and acne for HowStuffWorks and suggests a future episode on acne.

segments.title: Listener correction: Pilgrims versus Puritans
segments.summary: Listener Rachel writes that the hosts confused Pilgrims and Puritans in the America's Murderer episode. She says Pilgrims at Plymouth Rock were Separatists, while the Puritans who settled Massachusetts about ten years later wanted to reform the Church of England. The hosts say they are unsure and will look into it.
